# Nxeon — VPS hosting platform

Hostinger-style VPS hosting platform running on this Proxmox VE 9 dedicated server (OVH KS-GAME, i7-7700K, 64GB RAM, 2×450GB NVMe ZFS mirror + 4TB HDD backup pool).

## Architecture

- **Web panel**: Next.js 15 (App Router, server actions) + Tailwind v4, served by `nxeon-web.service` on port 3000, behind nginx on port 80. Public IP: 51.79.162.96.
- **Worker**: `worker/index.ts` run by `nxeon-worker.service` (as root — it manages iptables). Polls the `Job` table every 3s and executes provisioning/lifecycle jobs against the Proxmox API.
- **DB**: PostgreSQL 17, database `nxeon`, Prisma ORM ([prisma/schema.prisma](prisma/schema.prisma)). Use `npm run db:push` after schema changes.
- **Proxmox**: API token auth (`nxeon@pve!platform`, creds in `.env`). Templates: VMID 9000 (Ubuntu 24.04), 9001 (Debian 13), cloud-init based, cloned onto ZFS storage `vmdata`.
- **Networking**: VMs attach to NAT bridge `vmbr1` (10.20.0.0/24, gateway .1). IPs allocated from 10.20.0.100–250 ([lib/ipam.ts](lib/ipam.ts)). SSH exposed via DNAT port forwards 20000–29999 in iptables chain `NXEON_FWD`, rebuilt from DB by [worker/network.ts](worker/network.ts) — never edit that chain by hand.
- **Cloud-init**: vendor snippet at `/tank/backup/snippets/nxeon-vendor.yaml` (installs qemu-guest-agent, enables root password SSH).

## Portals & design system

**As of 2026-09-14, the customer portal is the "Nexion" redesign** — previously developed in isolation on a separate box (node-2, `/opt/nxeon-v2`, branch `design/v2`) and merged into `main` once it was fully audited and verified. Read this section before touching any shared styling — it is the difference between an edit that stays contained and one that silently reaches marketing, login, or admin.

- **Two portals, two shells, deliberately unmerged:**
  - `app/admin/**` (admin ops portal) still renders through `components/portal/Shell.tsx` — the ORIGINAL, pre-redesign chrome. Marketing (`app/(marketing)/**`), `/login`, `/register` and admin must stay pixel-identical to how they looked before the redesign. Never edit these expecting Nexion's visual language to apply, and never move Nexion-only styling into a place they can see it.
  - `app/dashboard/**` (customer portal) renders through `components/nx/Shell.tsx` — the Nexion redesign. This is where the new design system, its components (`components/nx/*`), and its color/animation language live.
  - **A component added to one shell must be added to the other if it's meant to exist on both.** This has silently broken things before: `ComposeProvider`, `TerminalDockProvider`, `MatrixProvider` were each added to `components/portal/Shell.tsx` first and forgotten on `components/nx/Shell.tsx`, taking a whole feature down invisibly (the crash only appeared on a route a smoke test didn't walk).

- **The scoping trick that keeps the two visually separate — `app/globals.css`, `:root:has(.nx-shell-root)`:**
  Nexion's own colors/tokens and its overrides of shared component classes (`.card`, `.btn-primary`, `.input`, etc.) are NOT bare rules — they're wrapped in `:root:has(.nx-shell-root) { ... }`, a selector that only matches when a `.nx-shell-root` element (rendered only by `components/nx/Shell.tsx`) exists anywhere on the page. That's the entire mechanism keeping marketing/login/admin rendering their original, pre-redesign styles: **do not write a new bare rule for a class both portals share** (e.g. a bare `.card { ... }` outside this scope) — it will apply everywhere, including where it was never meant to.
  - Light mode has its own nested scope for the same reason: `:root:has(.nx-shell-root)[data-theme="light"]`, NOT a bare `html[data-theme="light"]`. The bare form loses a CSS specificity fight to the dark `:has()` block regardless of which theme is active — this was a real, session-spanning bug (several "light mode doesn't work on page X" reports all had this one root cause) before it was scoped correctly.
  - `.nx-dark-island` is a third scope, deliberately staying dark inside the Nexion portal even when light mode is active (site headers, page hero banners) — it re-declares the relevant tokens back to dark values inside `html[data-theme="light"] .nx-dark-island { ... }`. Add a new always-dark token here too if you introduce one (see `--color-neon-bug` for the pattern: declared in the base `@theme` block, overridden lighter in the light-mode scope, re-declared back to its bright value inside `.nx-dark-island`).

- **CSS/JS landmines hit (and fixed) building this — avoid repeating them:**
  - **`@keyframes` and `@property` are not valid nested inside a plain style rule** — only inside `@layer`/`@media`/other at-rules. Nesting one inside `:root:has(...) { }` (or any class selector) silently drops it at build time — no error, the animation just never plays, forever, with every other signal (computed `animation-name`, `animation-play-state: running`) looking correct. This broke ~34 animations at once (a levitating icon, the page preloader, several status dots) when a broad `:has()` refactor accidentally wrapped them. If an animation looks "stuck on frame one," check whether its `@keyframes` block ended up nested inside a style rule.
  - **`backdrop-filter` on an ancestor creates a new containing block for `position: fixed` descendants.** A `.card` with `backdrop-blur-md` breaks any non-portaled modal/overlay nested inside it (it pins to the card instead of the viewport). Fix: cancel the inherited `backdrop-filter` on the offending class, or `createPortal` the fixed element to `document.body`.
  - **A positioned `fixed; z-0` decorative background (an aurora/globe effect) paints above ordinary static content** unless the real content wrapper gets `relative z-[1]`.
  - **Hydration-mismatch anti-pattern**: `useState(() => { if (typeof window === "undefined") return X; ...read window/URL...; return Y; })` — the server always takes the `X` branch, the client's first render always takes `Y`, guaranteed mismatch. Read the value server-side (a Server Component's `searchParams` prop) and pass it down as a real prop instead.
  - Percentage-based `transform: translateY(%)` inside a flex item whose container has no defined width/height resolves against 0 and silently does nothing — give the container a real dimension (e.g. `inset-0` instead of `inset-y-0 right-0` alone) before debugging the animation itself.
  - `git commit -m` with backticks in the message breaks — write the message to a file and use `git commit -F`.
  - Bash `cwd` does not persist between tool calls in an agent session — always `cd /opt/nxeon && ...` in the same command.

- Design system tokens/classes live in `app/globals.css` + `components/ui/primitives.tsx` (shared/production) and `components/nx/*` (Nexion-only). Charts are dependency-free SVG (`components/ui/charts.tsx`) — do not add a charting library.
- Admin impersonation: `impersonateUser()` sets a signed cookie; `currentUser()` returns the target, `realUser()` the actual admin; banner + exit handled in Shell. Admin pages call `realUser`/`requireAdmin` and refuse to render while impersonating.
- Metrics come from Proxmox RRD via `/api/metrics` (node for admins, per-server for owners). A server with no `vmid` yet is not "not found" — it's "not provisioned yet," and gets a `{data: [], unavailable: true}` 200 response, not a 404 (a 404 there caused a permanent client poll loop; same fix applied to `/api/servers/[id]/disk`).

## Working on this codebase — one tree, any session

`/opt/nxeon` (this directory, branch `main`) is the single source of truth. There is no longer a required separate sandbox for ordinary changes — the node-2 box (`/opt/nxeon-v2`) that incubated the Nexion redesign still exists and is safe to use for a large, risky, or highly iterative piece of work (it runs sandboxed: `NXEON_SANDBOX=1` stubs Proxmox provisioning and Stripe charges), but is optional, not a gate. Any session — this one or another — can edit `main` directly and ship through the pipeline below.

1. Edit, then `npx tsc --noEmit` before building anything.
2. `npm run build` locally only to catch build errors before pushing — do not restart production services from an ad hoc build in this directory (see Commands below); this is validation, not deployment.
3. Commit (small, real commits — the GitHub post-commit hook auto-pushes `origin`).
4. `scripts/deploy-staging.sh <ref>` — builds, migrates, and restarts staging (`:8080`) from that ref. **Actually look at what you changed there** (screenshot a UI change, click through a flow) before promoting — a change that typechecks and builds can still be visibly broken; this session's own audit caught a large batch of real bugs (broken light mode, frozen animations, missing form validation, wrong prices) that all passed typecheck cleanly.
5. `scripts/promote-production.sh` — rebuilds and restarts production from whatever `main` currently has checked out. It refuses to run if staging isn't healthy first.

If two sessions are likely to be editing at once, coordinate the ordinary way: pull before starting, small commits, push often (the auto-push hook does this for you on commit).

## Integrations (activate via /opt/nxeon/.env)

- **Stripe**: `STRIPE_SECRET_KEY` + `STRIPE_WEBHOOK_SECRET` → wallet top-ups switch from demo gateway to Checkout (`/api/stripe/checkout`, webhook `/api/stripe/webhook`, event `checkout.session.completed`, idempotent by session id). Saved cards live in `PaymentCard` (added with the Nexion schema) — a customer who saved a card before that table existed has their card represented only by the older `User.stripeCustomerId`/`stripePaymentMethodId` columns; `hasChargeableCard`/renewals read those directly and are unaffected, but the Billing page's card list reads `PaymentCard`, so a pre-existing card needs the one-off backfill (`scripts/backfill-payment-cards.ts`) to show up there. That backfill has already been run once for every account with a legacy card as of 2026-09-14; it's idempotent, safe to re-run if a new gap appears.
- **Namecheap** (`lib/namecheap.ts`): `NAMECHEAP_API_USER/KEY/USERNAME/CLIENT_IP` (+`NAMECHEAP_SANDBOX=1` for testing) → domain search/register/renew/DNS management. TLD retail prices in `TLD_PRICES`.
- **GitHub**: remote `origin` = `git@github.com:santino1233/nxeon.git` via deploy key `/root/.ssh/nxeon_deploy`. Every commit auto-pushes via `.git/hooks/post-commit`. `.env`/credentials are gitignored — never commit secrets.

## Conventions

- All state changes to VMs go through `Job` rows — the web app never calls Proxmox mutation endpoints directly (read-only status calls are OK).
- One in-flight job per server (enforced in `serverAction`).
- Admin-only actions live in [lib/actions.ts](lib/actions.ts) and must call `requireAdmin()`.
- Free VPSes: `Server.isFree = true`, no billing, `expiresAt = null`.
- Wallet amounts are integer cents.
- Never fabricate: no invented stats, ratings, reviews, player counts, or ETAs. If a number can't be read from the database or a real upstream, the field stays empty and the UI says why — this tree has had hash-derived star ratings and fake reviews removed once already.
- Minecraft subdomains (`*.play.nxeon.cloud`) are shared across two tables — `FreeMinecraftServer.subdomain` and `Server.subdomain` — because both products resolve under the same DNS zone. Always check availability through `lib/game-subdomain.ts`'s `isSubdomainAvailable()` (queries both) rather than checking either table alone, or a free and a paid server can claim the same name.

## Documentation — keep it current (required)

content.thinking:
I'm checking how the partners page formats currency and money values so I stay consistent, then planning a new admin-only data module for partner program analytics that reuses the range and bucketing helpers from the existing partner analytics library.

Since those bucket helpers aren't currently exported, I'll add export keywords to them rather than duplicate the logic — a small, low-risk change. Then I'm working through the headline metrics: defaulting the range to "all" given how young the program is, and defining the first card around link clicks with a breakdown of unique visitors based on hashed IPs.

I'm also noting a footnote for clicks on codes that don't map to an actual partner, and sketching out the rest of the metrics — new attached customers, first paying customers, referred revenue, commission earned, and payouts, each scoped to the selected range, plus a separate lifetime ledger for earned, paid, and outstanding totals that stays program-wide regardless of range.

For charts, I'm thinking through how to visualize traffic and conversions over time — probably separate charts for link clicks versus new customer/conversion counts, since clicks vastly outnumber signups and combining them on one scale would flatten the smaller series.

I also need to figure out how to thin the x-axis labels for buckets like 46 daily points, since the chart evenly spaces whatever labels I pass regardless of the underlying data count — I'll need to pick a subset of labels at roughly evenly-spaced data indices so they align correctly with the plotted points.

I'm also weighing whether area charts are even the right choice here, since smoothing between sparse daily counts can misleadingly render a single day's activity as a hump spanning neighboring days — a bar chart might better represent discrete per-bucket counts.

Checking the codebase convention: it requires dependency-free SVG charts in charts.tsx, no external libraries. There's also a separate client-side BarChart component tied to Nexion theme variables, but mixing its cyan/violet styling into the admin's slate/brand aesthetic would look inconsistent, so I'll stick with the AreaChart from charts.tsx to match admin conventions.

For commission trends, even sparse data with mostly zeros and occasional spikes will render fine as an area chart. I'll show cumulative lines for earned vs. paid commission — running totals calculated from the program's start rather than just the visible range, so the gap between lines meaningfully represents outstanding liability.

I'm settling on four charts: link clicks per bucket, new customers vs paying conversions, commission earned vs paid out as a running total, and possibly referred revenue vs commission per bucket. I also want a funnel card showing click → signup → paying, while being upfront that attribution between clicks and signups is inherently weak.

For the funnel, I'm breaking it into link clicks with unique visitors, attached customers split by whether they came through a tracked click match versus a new or later-attached account, and paying customers based on cohort — those with at least one non-void commission. Rather than showing a misleading conversion rate like signups/clicks, I want to be explicit: show "clicks matched to a signup" as the true attributed rate, and label any other ratios clearly as ratios rather than conversion rates.

For signup-to-paying, I'll show the cohort count who eventually paid — right now that's 3 of 5 partners (ACME, SSSS, AWESOME) all-time. Then I'm designing a per-partner ranking table with clicks, attached customers, paying customers, referred revenue, commission earned, and all-time owed, sorted by revenue with a MeterBar for share and links to each partner's admin page.

I also want a "where clicks come from" breakdown by referer host, plus a lightweight "product mix" section showing commission and revenue by product category since I'm already fetching invoices. I'm checking whether discount cost is trackable — invoices don't seem to have a typed discount field, so I may need to skip that or note it as untracked.

For recruitment, I can pull real numbers from PartnerInvite records (kind CREATOR): sent, claimed, pending, revoked/expired. I'll keep it simple using creatorInviteState rather than pulling EmailLog opens, and treat this as an all-time metric rather than range-based since invites track lastSentAt/acceptedAt independently.

For partner activity, I want a compact activation metric like "8 partners · 2 had clicks in range · 4 have customers · 3 have earned commission" — real and simple to compute. For click volume I'll fetch ReferralClick data (createdAt, code, ipHash, referer, convertedUserId) capped at 100k like the partner module, and pull invoices for attached customers to measure referred revenue.

Rather than filtering by a large list of userIds, I should query with a relation filter for customers who have a partner attachment, matching what the reconcile sweep does, then join attachment data in memory. I need to be careful that revenue calculations respect the same future-only attribution rule as commissions — comparing invoice createdAt against attachment createdAt — and I'm now considering whether detached customers should still count toward revenue since detaching removes the PartnerC... relationship.

For refunds, I'll sum refundedCents on paid commissionable invoices plus amounts from REFUNDED-status invoices within range, displaying a "Refunded" line only when nonzero along with a note that commissions aren't automatically reversed for refunds.

Good news: the actual data shows zero refunds for partner customers, which simplifies things. I'll define referred revenue as the net pre-tax amount of every PAID, positive, non-top-up invoice a partner-attached customer was charged on or after attachment — the same base commission is computed on — with fully refunded invoices dropping out and partial refunds on still-PAID invoices subtracted. I should also flag that commission isn't reversed by a refund since there's no code path that voids a PartnerCommission, and I want to double-check the refundedCents semantics by checking the refund action code.

content.thinking:
I'm working through how refunds should net against tax: since refundedCents is tracked as a gross figure against amountCents, I need to scale it down proportionally by the net-to-gross ratio to get the actual revenue impact, keeping the calculation simple by summing net amounts over paid commissionable invoices and then subtracting proportional refunds for both partial and full cases.

Given the messiness of credit-note REFUNDED invoices (where refundedCents might be zero and amountCents itself represents the refund), I've decided to keep revenue calculation simple and not net out refunds at all -- instead I'll define referred revenue as net charges that earned or would earn commission, and add an honest UI footnote noting that refunds aren't reflected in these numbers and don't currently reverse commissions either, while flagging the commission-reversal gap in the report and docs.

For "paying customers," I'm weighing two definitions: customers with at least one non-VOID commission row, matching the existing funnel logic, versus customers with at least one paid commissionable invoice since attach, which stays consistent with my revenue definition but includes charges made under paused partners.

I'll go with the invoice-based definition since it's the truer "paying customer" concept — currently both approaches agree at 3 customers, but they'd diverge for paused partners, zero-rate commissions, or dedicated-IP-only purchases. This means "first paid purchase" date should also be the first commissionable invoice since attach, and I'm confirming that a discounted first purchase still counts as long as it's a PAID invoice with a positive amount.

For the "new vs existing account" classification, I'm using a 10-minute window between account creation and attachment to flag "new account at signup" — but testing this against AWESOME's case (user created at 17:43:53, attached 7.7 minutes later via checkout code) raises a question about whether that's a fair label, since the customer is genuinely new but the attachment happened slightly after signup rather than at the exact moment.

I'm settling on a 24-hour threshold instead: accounts created within 24 hours of attachment count as "new customers," while ZEUS's August accounts and ACME's July accounts (both clearly pre-existing) count as "existing." This gives a clean, defensible definition — new accounts are ones created within 24h of being attached, existing accounts are older ones attached later via admin action or a code entered at a subsequent checkout.

For the "matched to a tracked click" count, I'm checking which attached customers have their ID in the referral click's converted-user field — currently that's zero, which checks out since the SSSS signup used a typed code (a removed feature) rather than a tracked click.

Now I'm laying out the per-partner table columns scoped to the selected date range: partner name/code/status, rate, clicks, new customers attached in that range, paying customers, referred revenue, commission, and all-time amount owed, sorted by referred revenue descending with ties broken by commission, clicks, then name. I'm still deciding how to define "paying" in this table — likely based on first purchase within the range.

I'm working through two different definitions to avoid confusion: the top-level cards should show "paying customers" as those whose first commissionable purchase since attach fell in the selected range, while the funnel card should instead track a cohort — customers attached in the range and whether they've paid at any point since, which is the more honest funnel view. I'm leaning toward keeping these two clearly labeled rather than merging them.

Next I should check what the referer data looks like in production clicks to understand what traffic sources are actually populated.

I'm now defining the type shapes for the series points and partner rows — tracking clicks, revenue, commission, payouts, and cumulative earned/paid totals over time, plus a summary row per partner including lifetime earnings and amount still owed.

I'm working through the invites summary shape and clarifying that "claimedWithClick" means accepted creator invites whose linked partner has at least one click all-time. I also need to make sure unique visitors are computed as distinct ipHash values across the whole range rather than summed per partner, while per-partner unique visitors get their own distinct ipHash count.

For structuring the code, I'm deciding whether to split partner loading, earliest-activity lookup, and analytics computation into separate functions, or combine everything—including range resolution—into one function that the page can call directly, which seems simpler overall.

Now I'm planning the queries: pulling click records within the date range with fields like code, timestamp, ipHash, referer, and converted user; grouping clicks by code across all time to get counts and earliest activity; counting clicks from codes outside the partner set within the range; and looking up customer attachments.

Still defining queries...

I'm also considering invites, which aren't filtered by partner since recruitment is program-level, but I need to figure out how to handle claimedWithClick for hidden partners — likely by pulling all-time click counts across all codes rather than just the filtered partner set.

For qualifying invoices, I'm mapping each customer to their attachment record and filtering invoices to those that are commissionable and occurred after attachment, then determining the customer's first purchase timestamp as the earliest such invoice date. Revenue is summed per partner, bucket, and product for invoices in range, while first-purchase detection still checks all invoices before the range end to correctly identify true first purchases.

I'm reconsidering the cohort logic: customers attached within the range count as new customers, but determining if they've "paid" should probably look at all-time invoices rather than bounding by the range end, so I'll fetch invoices without the upper time restriction, compute first-purchase timestamps across all time, and separately track which of those first purchases fall within the selected range for reporting revenue and paid-cohort counts.

Now I'm defining newAccount as attachments happening within 24 hours of customer creation, and matchedClick as the set of converted user IDs pulled from all referral clicks tied to the partner's codes (not just within the range) so I can properly attribute in-range attachments — making sure the click's code matches the specific partner's code for correctness.

For the per-bucket series, I'm computing cumulative earned and paid amounts by summing commissions up through each bucket, using an index map similar to how partner-analytics does it. For the ledger, I'm calculating all-time totals: earned (sum of non-void commissions), paidOut (sum of payouts), and owed per partner as the max of zero or earned minus paid, while also tracking accrued and paid row totals separately so I can flag a discrepancy hint if they don't match the "owed" figure shown elsewhere.

I'm also mapping click referrers to sources, and product descriptions to privacy-friendly generic labels (like "Game server · Minecraft" or "VPS") to compute revenue and counts per product within the date range. Then I'm building per-partner rows sorted by revenue, commission, new customers, clicks, and name, plus a summary of partner counts by status, click activity, and customer activity.

For safety I'm handling the empty-codes edge case, capping range clicks at 200k with a truncation flag if exceeded, and now I'm putting it all together into the final file.

content.content:
(`lib/partner-commission.ts`, pure, unit-tested) = `max(0, netCents − dedicatedIpCents)`. Every
accrual path (`accrueCommissionForInvoice`, called by the inline post-order/post-renewal hooks AND
the background `reconcilePartnerCommissions` sweep) reads `Invoice.dedicatedIpCents` and excludes it
— never a string match against a line-item description.

**Admin** (`/admin/partners`, `/admin/partners/[id]`, `lib/actions-partner.ts`,
`components/admin/PartnerControls.tsx`): create/manage partners and rates (existing), attach/detach
customers (existing), plus new: real click→signup→conversion funnel (`partnerFunnel`), the real
`/partner/<code>` link, **invite a brand-new login** (`adminCreatePartnerInvite` — a public accept
page at `/partner/invite/accept?token=...` creates the account, since the invitee has none yet;
mirrors `OrgInvite`'s token/hash/expiry, not its `requireUser()`-gated redemption), and **record a
partial/specific payout** (`adminRecordPartnerPayout`) alongside the existing full-settle
(`adminSettlePartnerCommission`, now payout-ledger-aware).

**Partner portal — tabs (2026-09-27).** `/dashboard/partner` is split into seven tabs driven by
`?tab=` (linkable, survives refresh; resolved server-side in `app/dashboard/partner/page.tsx`, then
the client switches tabs with the native History API so no server round trip is needed; a
WAI-ARIA tablist with roving focus — ←/→/Home/End). Tab list: `lib/nx/partner-tabs.ts`.

entries.name: Monitor
entries.description:
Start a background monitor that streams events from a long-running script. Each stdout line is an event — you keep working and notifications arrive in the chat. Events arrive on their own schedule and are not replies from the user, even if one lands while you're waiting for the user to answer a question.

Pick by how many notifications you need:
- **One** ("tell me when the server is ready / the build finishes") → use **Bash with `run_in_background`** and a command that exits when the condition is true, e.g. `until grep -q "Ready in" dev.log; do sleep 0.5; done`. You get a single completion notification when it exits.
- **One per occurrence, until the monitor expires (re-arm to continue)** ("tell me every time an ERROR line appears") → Monitor with an unbounded command (`tail -f`, `inotifywait -m`, `while true`).
- **One per occurrence, until a known end** ("emit each CI step result, stop when the run completes") → Monitor with a command that emits lines and then exits.

Your script's stdout is the event stream. Each line becomes a notification. Exit ends the watch.

  # Each matching log line is an event
  tail -f /var/log/app.log | grep --line-buffered "ERROR"

  # Each file change is an event
  inotifywait -m --format '%e %f' /watched/dir

  # Poll GitHub for new PR comments and emit one line per new comment
  last=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)
  while true; do
    now=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)
    gh api "repos/owner/repo/issues/123/comments?since=$last" --jq '.[] | "\(.user.login): \(.body)"'
    last=$now; sleep 30
  done

  # Node script that emits events as they arrive (e.g. WebSocket listener)
  node watch-for-events.js

  # Per-occurrence with a natural end: emit each CI check as it lands, exit when the run completes
  prev=""
  while true; do
    s=$(gh pr checks 123 --json name,bucket)
    cur=$(jq -r '.[] | select(.bucket!="pending") | "\(.name): \(.bucket)"' <<<"$s" | sort)
    comm -13 <(echo "$prev") <(echo "$cur")
    prev=$cur
    jq -e 'all(.bucket!="pending")' <<<"$s" >/dev/null && break
    sleep 30
  done

**Don't use an unbounded command for a single notification.** `tail -f`, `inotifywait -m`, and `while true` never exit on their own, so the monitor stays armed until timeout even after the event has fired. For "tell me when X is ready," use Bash `run_in_background` with an `until` loop instead (one notification, ends in seconds). Note that `tail -f log | grep -m 1 ...` does *not* fix this: if the log goes quiet after the match, `tail` never receives SIGPIPE and the pipeline hangs anyway.

**Script quality:**
- Every pipe stage must flush per line or matches sit in its buffer unseen: `grep` needs `--line-buffered`, `awk` needs `fflush()`. `head` cannot flush at all — `| head -N` delivers nothing until N matches accumulate, then ends the stream.
- In poll loops, handle transient failures (`curl ... || true`) — one failed request shouldn't kill the monitor.
- Poll intervals: 30s+ for remote APIs (rate limits), 0.5-1s for local checks.
- Write a specific `description` — it appears in every notification ("errors in deploy.log" not "watching logs").
- Only stdout is the event stream. Stderr goes to the output file (readable via Read) but does not trigger notifications — for a command you run directly (e.g. `python train.py 2>&1 | grep --line-buffered ...`), merge stderr with `2>&1` so its failures reach your filter. (No effect on `tail -f` of an existing log — that file only contains what its writer redirected.)

**Coverage — silence is not success.** When watching a job or process for an outcome, your filter must match every terminal state, not just the happy path. A monitor that greps only for the success marker stays silent through a crashloop, a hung process, or an unexpected exit — and silence looks identical to "still running." Before arming, ask: *if this process crashed right now, would my filter emit anything?* If not, widen it.

  # Wrong — silent on crash, hang, or any non-success exit
  tail -f run.log | grep --line-buffered "elapsed_steps="

  # Right — one alternation covering progress + the failure signatures you'd act on
  tail -f run.log | grep -E --line-buffered "elapsed_steps=|Traceback|Error|FAILED|assert|Killed|OOM"

For poll loops checking job state, emit on every terminal status (`succeeded|failed|cancelled|timeout`), not just success. If you cannot confidently enumerate the failure signatures, broaden the grep alternation rather than narrow it — some extra noise is better than missing a crashloop.

**Output volume**: Every stdout line is a conversation message, so the filter should be selective — but selective means "the lines you'd act on," not "only good news." Never pipe raw logs; filter to exactly the success and failure signals you care about. Monitors that produce too many events are automatically stopped; restart with a tighter filter if this happens.

Stdout lines within 200ms are batched into a single notification, so multiline output from a single event groups naturally.

The script runs in the same shell environment as Bash. Exit ends the watch (exit code is reported). Every monitor expires after `timeout_ms` (default 5 minutes, at most 30 minutes): it is killed and you get one notice with the event count. Re-arm it if you still need the watch; for a long watch (PR monitoring, log tails) set `timeout_ms` to the maximum and re-arm on each expiry, and widen the filter if an expiry with no events was unexpected. Use TaskStop to cancel early.
**ws source** — open a WebSocket and stream each incoming text frame as an event. No shell, no polling: the server pushes, you get notified.

  Monitor({
    ws: {url: 'wss://events.example.com/stream', protocols: ['v1']},
    description: 'deploy events',
  })

Each text frame becomes one notification (multiline frames stay as one event). Binary frames are reported as `[binary frame, N bytes]` rather than passed through. Socket close ends the watch with the close code surfaced; errors are surfaced before close. Same rate limiting as bash — a firehose will be suppressed and eventually stopped, so subscribe to a filtered feed where one exists.

Prefer this over `command: 'websocat wss://…'` — it avoids the extra process and line-buffering pitfalls. Use bash when you need to transform or filter frames with shell tools before they become events.

description.description: Short human-readable description of what you are monitoring (shown in notifications).

timeout_ms.description: Kill the monitor after this deadline. Default 300000ms. Deadlines above 1800000ms are capped to 1800000ms. You are notified at expiry and can re-arm.

command.description: Shell command or script. Each stdout line is an event; exit ends the watch.

ws.description: WebSocket to open. Each text frame is an event; binary frames are reported as a placeholder line. Socket close ends the watch. Cannot be combined with command.

For thinning labels when there are many data points, I'm working out a spacing algorithm: pick every kth index (k scaled to number of points, capped around 6 labels), always include the last index, and drop a label if it lands too close to its neighbor to avoid overlapping text.

input.title: Void partner commission when a charge is refunded
input.tldr: While building the partner analytics I found that refunding an invoice never reverses the partner commission accrued on it, so a creator can be paid on money Nxeon gave back. This task adds that reversal.
input.prompt:
Nxeon (repo /opt/nxeon, Next.js 15 + Prisma; read CLAUDE.md first — work in a git worktree, never run `npm run build` in /opt/nxeon, typecheck with `npx tsc --noEmit`, deploy via scripts/deploy-staging.sh, update docs/DOCUMENTATION.md + ROADMAP.md, do NOT merge/promote without the owner's sign-off).

Problem: Creator Partner Program commissions (`PartnerCommission`, prisma/schema.prisma; accrued by lib/partner-commission.ts `accrueCommissionForInvoice` for every PAID, positive, non-top-up invoice of a partner-attached customer) are never reversed when that invoice is refunded. Nothing in the codebase sets `PartnerCommission.status = "VOID"` (grep confirms: VOID is only read, never written). Refund paths that should be considered:
- lib/actions-admin-billing.ts refund action — increments `Invoice.refundedCents` via compare-and-swap and flips `Invoice.status` to REFUNDED once refundedCents >= amountCents (partial refunds leave it PAID).
- lib/actions-server-lifecycle.ts (~line 445) immediate-cancel refund — writes a separate "credit note" invoice with status REFUNDED and a positive amountCents.
- lib/domain-transfer.ts (~line 129) — flips the original PAID invoice to REFUNDED.
- lib/server-spend.ts documents these representations in detail.

Decide with the owner how partial refunds should work (pro-rate the commission vs void only on full refund), and whether an ACCRUED commission vs an already-PAID one (a payout was recorded — see PartnerPayout and computePartnerSummary, balance = earned − payouts) should be handled differently (e.g. a negative adjustment row rather than mutating a paid row). Implement the agreed rule idempotently in the refund paths, add a unit test, and make sure the admin Partners Overview tab (app/admin/partners/ProgramOverview.tsx / lib/partner-program-analytics.ts, on branch feature/partner-analytics if not yet merged) and the partner dashboard (lib/partner-analytics.ts) still read correctly — both already exclude VOID rows. As of 2026-09-29 no partner-attached customer has a refunded invoice in prod, so there is nothing to backfill yet — verify that before shipping.

input.title: Credit partner-link clicks for checkout-code attaches
input.tldr: The new partner analytics show 0 of 9 real link clicks matched to a signup, because customers who type a creator code at checkout never get their earlier click credited. This task fixes that attribution.
input.prompt:
Nxeon (repo /opt/nxeon; read CLAUDE.md first — work in a git worktree, never `npm run build` in /opt/nxeon, `npx tsc --noEmit`, stage via scripts/deploy-staging.sh, update docs/DOCUMENTATION.md + ROADMAP.md, don't merge/promote without owner sign-off).

Context: partner link visits are recorded in `ReferralClick` (app/partner/[code]/route.ts and app/r/[code]/route.ts store code, a salted `ipHash` via lib/coupon-order.ts `hashIp(clientIp(headers), AUTH_SECRET)`, referer). `ReferralClick.convertedUserId` is only set by lib/partner-commission.ts `attachCustomerToPartnerByCode` (link-cookie signups via register / Google / Discord), which credits the newest unmatched click for that code. The OTHER attach path — the deploy wizard promo box, lib/creator-code.ts `attachCreatorCode` via lib/actions-creator-code.ts — never marks a click, so the admin Partners > Overview funnel (lib/partner-program-analytics.ts, branch feature/partner-analytics) shows "clicks matched to a signup: 0 of 9". A real prod case: the AWESOME partner's customer clicked the link 2026-09-28 17:24–17:36 UTC, signed up with Google at 17:43 (before the OAuth callbacks read the cookie, fixed in f9d2acd688), then typed the code at checkout at 17:51.

Task: when attachCreatorCode succeeds, best-effort mark a matching unconverted ReferralClick as converted — prefer a click with the SAME ipHash (compute it the same way the click route does from the server action's request headers) within a sensible window (e.g. 30 days, matching the nxeon_ref cookie TTL), and do NOT fall back to crediting an arbitrary click from a different IP (that would inflate the funnel). Never block the attach on it. Consider whether a one-off backfill for existing checkout-code attaches (AuditLog action "partner.customer_attached", detail "code=X via=checkout-code") is appropriate — dry-run it and show the owner before writing. Add a test for the matching rule.

input.message:
## Partner analytics + Partners page reorganization: done, pushed, not merged

**Branch:** `feature/partner-analytics`, pushed to origin, HEAD `fe5dfade58`. It contains commit 6c83cad830 and current main (9481536b7e), and merges cleanly into main. I have **not** merged it into main or promoted it to production; that's the owner's call. Worktree: `/root/nxeon-worktrees/partner-analytics`.

One gap first: I could not visually check the real staging admin page while logged in. The staging admin password in `/root/nxeon-staging-credentials.txt` is stale (the login returns "Invalid email or password"). My attempt to create a short-lived staging session token was denied by the permission system, and I didn't pursue it further. The Overview tab was checked visually another way (see Verification). The Partners and Creator invites tabs were not seen in a browser.

### How the page is organized now
`/admin/partners` has three tabs inside the page, using the same `?tab=` strip as `/admin/logs`. I didn't use the shared SubTabs bar, as you asked. Only the active tab loads its data.
- **Overview** (the default): the new program-wide analytics.
- **Partners** (`?tab=partners`): the all-partners table, then "Add a partner". The partner detail page's breadcrumb now returns here.
- **Creator invites** (`?tab=invites`): new recruitment figures (invites / drafts / sent and waiting / claimed / expired or revoked / claimed creators who've had a click), then the invite form, then the invites table.
- Tab labels show real counts, e.g. "Creator invites 15".
- The existing tables, forms and your `startsWith` invite-status fix are moved across unchanged. The sidebar entry from 6c83cad830 is untouched.

### What the Overview shows
**All time:**
- Partners: 8 (8 active, 2 with a link click, 4 with customers, 3 earning).
- Commission earned $21.35, paid out $0.00, owed $21.35.
- "Owed" is each partner's earned commission minus the payouts recorded for them, the same balance their Manage page shows.

**For a chosen range** (7d / 30d / 90d / 12m / all time / custom; defaults to all time):
- Six headline figures:
  - link clicks and unique visitors
  - customers attached, split into new accounts and existing ones
  - paying customers
  - referred revenue (after tax)
  - commission
  - paid out
- Four trend charts:
  - clicks
  - customers attached vs. first purchases
  - revenue vs. commission
  - running totals of earned vs. paid out

  Plus a table of every day/week behind them.
- A click → signup → paying funnel.
- Referred revenue by product.
- Where clicks come from.
- Partners ranked by referred revenue.
- A "hide partners" filter. There's no test flag on partners, and ACME ("Test Agency") and SSSS ("Test") look like internal tests that make up most of the commission.

### What's backed by real data, and the gaps
Every number is a count or sum from a real table. Referred revenue uses exactly the rules commission uses (paid, positive, not a wallet top-up, dated at or after the customer was attached). Refunds are not subtracted, and the page says so. Checked against the live database (read-only): $21.35 matches the old "Accrued (unpaid)" card, and all other figures match direct SQL. That's $45.88 revenue over 12 charges and 9 partner-link clicks from 5 unique IPs. One more click was on a code that isn't a partner's; it's excluded and noted. There are 5 attached customers (2 new, 3 existing) and 3 paying.

These gaps are shown on the page rather than hidden:
- **0 of 9 clicks are matched to a signup.** Only accounts created through the link itself get a click credited. I traced every case:
  - AWESOME's customer clicked the link, signed up with Google before the Google/Discord sign-ins read the partner cookie (fixed in f9d2acd688), then typed the code at checkout. That checkout path never credits a click.
  - SSSS's customer used the typed signup field that has since been removed.
  - The other three were attached by an admin.

  So "customers attached" is not a click-through rate.
- **No click has recorded a referring site**, so every click shows as "Direct / not shared".
- **Refunds never reverse a commission.** Nothing in the code ever marks a commission void. This is a real money-path bug, not just an analytics gap.

I flagged the refund bug and the click-matching gap as separate follow-up tasks.

### Other changes
- `components/ui/charts.tsx`: the first and last x-axis labels on the shared chart now anchor inward, so a date at the right edge isn't cut in half. This affects every page that uses that chart.
- `lib/partner-analytics.ts`: now exports its date-bucket helpers for reuse; no behaviour change.
- `docs/DOCUMENTATION.md` and `ROADMAP.md` are updated. I didn't run `publish-docs.mjs`, because that would publish unmerged docs; run it after merging.

### Verification
- **Typecheck:** `npx tsc --noEmit` passes.
- **Staging:** deployed twice via `scripts/deploy-staging.sh`. Staging now runs `fe5dfade`, the build passes, it returns HTTP 200, all three tab URLs redirect to login when signed out, and there are no new errors in the staging log.
- **Overview visual check:** I rendered it with the real production data and staging's compiled CSS, then screenshotted it at 1440px and 390px wide. Everything was right except two layout bugs, both fixed:
  - 156px of sideways page scroll on phones.
  - Clipped or misaligned chart dates.

  The invalid custom range shows its warning and falls back to 30 days. On the live database, the custom-range and hide filters produced correct numbers.
- **Not browser-checked:** the Partners and Creator invites tabs, because of the login problem above. They're the existing markup moved, plus the recruitment card.

### To do
- **Look at staging while logged in** at `https://staging.4j3d7gkr2wcbi34.nxeon.cloud/admin/partners`. Note that `staging.nxeon.cloud/admin` returns 404. This needs a working staging admin login.
- **Staging credentials:** fix the stale `/root/nxeon-staging-credentials.txt` or reset that admin's password. Resetting a password is a credential change, so it's your decision.
- **Leftover scratchpad file:** `stg-admin.txt` in my scratchpad holds the staging admin's user id and role (no secret). My attempt to delete it was also blocked, so it's still there.
